items.body: Mala Fama‘s Río Cayápas and NXDLLI offer two complementary readings of the same journey. Both emerged from Esteban Farinango’s time in the Afro-Ecuadorian community of Telembí in Esmeraldas and were developed simultaneously, before OTONO label head Luis Clériga suggested presenting them as a double release. Río Cayápas stays close to communal music-making, while NXDLLI carries traces of these experiences into more abstract and introspective territory. Río Cayápas makes its intentions immediately clear. It opens with field recordings that place the listener in a specific environment before entering into what the liner notes describe as a dialogue with “local ethnic and autochthonous sounds.” Traditional rhythms from the province of Esmeraldas, recorded in the Telembí community, provide the foundation. Electronics work closely within this material, reinforcing percussion, marimba and voices until the boundaries between acoustic performance and electronic intervention become difficult to locate. NXDLLI turns towards resonance, atmosphere and slowly shifting textures, with rhythm largely receding from view. Recordings made in Esteban’s hometown of Ibarra filter quietly through the album, sometimes almost imperceptibly, particularly in “wakay”, “minervita” and “AMSA”. Environmental sounds become fragments of acoustic memory, retaining a connection to place even as their original context grows indistinct. Heard together, the two records continually illuminate one another. Río Cayápas foregrounds community, ritual and embodied rhythm; NXDLLI draws those experiences into introspective electroacoustic landscapes. Their shared sources make the differences between them all the more revealing. The accompanying remix collection demonstrates how much possibility remains within Mala Fama’s material. Each contributor finds something different in the originals. Entrañas draws out memory and dream; Omaar pushes the rhythms towards deconstructed bass; The Hissed finds unexpected harmonic warmth through ambient drum & bass; Viiaan turns birdsong into the principal melodic voice; Siete Catorce amplifies the ritual energy already embedded in the percussion; DNZA reveals surprising correspondences between Afro-Ecuadorian rhythms and footwork; and Quixosis dissolves the project into ambient resonance, bringing it close once again to landscape. Across both albums, traditional and electronic elements share the same musical space without settling into a clear hierarchy. Farinango allows percussion, marimba, voices, field recordings and electronics to interact until their respective roles become increasingly porous. Río Cayápas and NXDLLI trace the same journey through northern Ecuador from different perspectives, preserving the immediacy of encounters in Telembí alongside the altered forms those experiences assume through distance and memory. To trace the river back to its source, I caught up with Esteban over Zoom. NXDLLI and Río Cayápas explore the same path from two distinct perspectives. One is more closely linked to electroacoustic experimentation and ambient textures; the other foregrounds the music and rituals of Esmeraldas. At what point did you realize that this project needed to be divided into two releases? Was this an idea that was present from the beginning or did it emerge naturally during the creative process? My creative process isn’t linear. I never begin by thinking, I’m going to make an album. I’m always collecting sounds. Wherever I go, I record things that interest me because I’m constantly looking for material to experiment with. When I travelled to Esmeraldas and spent time in an Afro-Ecuadorian community, I recorded field recordings, instruments and all kinds of everyday sounds. From the beginning, I wanted to create something that captured the atmosphere of that place. A lot of projects combine electronic music with traditional music, but the two often remain separate—as if the electronics exist on one side and the traditional instruments on the other. I wanted to avoid that. My intention was to preserve the roots of the music while introducing just enough electronics to place it within a contemporary context. To me, that approach makes the music feel more alive. I love techno and electronic music, but sometimes purely electronic music can feel a little soulless. I wanted the electronics to support the traditional music rather than dominate it. At first, I was simply planning to make an EP. Around that time I received a grant from SAYCE—the Ecuadorian authors’ and composers’ society—which allowed me to develop the project properly. I initially wrote three tracks based on the material I had recorded in Esmeraldas. At the same time, though, I was recording completely different sounds closer to home. My grandmother would take me to waterfalls and perform prayers for my journey, surrounding me with flowers and blessings. I recorded her voice, the river, the birds—everything around us. Those recordings gradually led me towards another idea: creating long, ambient pieces built from atmosphere rather than rhythm. So I found myself working on two projects simultaneously. Then I met Luis Clériga from the Mexican label Otono. I told him about both projects: the rhythmically driven EP inspired by Esmeraldas and this second collection of ambient pieces. He immediately suggested combining them into a single release, with one side dedicated to the Afro-Ecuadorian, percussion-based material and the other exploring the more ambient, electroacoustic side. I thought it made perfect sense because the contrast between the two approaches actually revealed that they belonged to the same creative process. So, in the end, dividing the project into two complementary releases wasn’t my original idea—it was Luis’s. As soon as he suggested it, though, I realised it was exactly the right way to present the music. The Cayápas River and the Telembí community occupy a central place in both albums, but they never appear as mere backdrops or soundscapes. They become spaces of memory, ritual, and imagination. During your time there, was there any sound, encounter, or experience that decisively changed the course of the project? Everything was new to me. Even getting there felt like part of the experience. You can’t reach the community by road—you have to travel for almost three hours by boat before disappearing into the jungle. Once you’re there, there’s no phone signal. They have generators, but electricity isn’t available all the time, so you’re completely disconnected. At the same time, the place is incredibly abundant. Fruit trees are everywhere. You walk around, pick a banana, a mango or some cacao straight from the trees, go down to the river and start fishing. There’s a real sense of living alongside nature. But it’s also an extremely poor community. That’s the contradiction. Everything is beautiful, yet people have very limited access to basic services because they’re so remote. The government has largely forgotten them. What really struck me was meeting the local marimba maker. He’s a remarkable luthier whose instruments are highly sought after by musicians from outside the community. He harvests all the wood himself and builds every instrument by hand, yet he receives almost no recognition or support. Seeing that made me realise there was a political dimension to what I was experiencing. I felt incredibly fortunate to be there and to learn from them, and I also felt a responsibility to tell people how they live, what their music sounds like and what that community means—from my own perspective, of course. What impressed me most wasn’t just the landscape but the people themselves. In many ways they’re incredibly rich without necessarily thinking of themselves that way. They live surrounded by fruit, by the river, by music. People are constantly singing or playing drums, and music is woven into everyday life. They also have an extraordinary number of musical traditions connected to different moments of community life. During funerals, for example, women perform beautiful vocal chants that I would love to record one day. Unfortunately, when I visited there weren’t any ceremonies taking place, so I couldn’t document them. There are other celebrations where musicians travel along the river at night in boats, playing marimba and drums as they move through the water. They also have ceremonies where people dress in costumes made from leaves, preserving traditions that clearly trace back to their African heritage. What amazed me was that all of this exists just a few hours from where I live, yet most people in Ecuador know very little about it. That became one of my motivations for the project: to learn as much as I could and to show that this small country contains an extraordinary diversity of cultures that deserve to be heard. The visit itself happened thanks to a friend of mine, DJ Mamba System. He had already been there several times because he bought a marimba from the local luthier, so he knew the community well. You can’t simply book a hotel or arrange a visit online. You need to know someone. Families welcome you into their homes, often without expecting anything in return. My friend invited me to come with him, introduced me to everyone, and that’s how the whole experience began. They were incredibly generous people, and we became friends very quickly. So this might be a bit of a silly question, but do they have their own language? They speak Spanish, but some words and expressions in their songs come from Yoruba, reflecting their African heritage. It isn’t a language they use in everyday conversation, but traces of it survive in the music. What’s really interesting is that they share the region with an Indigenous community. I can’t remember the name right now (CHACHIS), but they’ve lived alongside each other for generations. As a result, some people also speak the Indigenous language, and the two cultures have influenced one another over a very long period. The history behind that is fascinating. A slave ship was wrecked off the Ecuadorian coast, and many of the enslaved Africans managed to escape. They fled into the jungle, where they eventually encountered the Indigenous communities already living there. From that point on, they shared knowledge, traditions and ways of life. You can actually hear that history in the music. Some of the melodic patterns in Afro-Ecuadorian traditions closely resemble those found in Indigenous music, so there’s this beautiful cultural exchange embedded in the sound itself. Did they find it strange that an electronic musician had come all that way to learn from them? Not really. To be honest, I don’t even think of myself as a purely electronic musician. I also play guitar and work with acoustic instruments, so our conversations naturally revolved around their music rather than mine. I did play them some of my work. They thought it was nice, but they weren’t especially interested in the electronic aspect of it—and that’s completely understandable. They simply said, “That’s cool. Thanks for coming.” What mattered much more to them was sharing their own musical traditions. They have an extraordinary number of rhythms and musical practices that very few people know about, and they’re genuinely happy when someone wants to listen and help bring that music beyond the community. In the end, that became my role: not to introduce them to electronic music, but to help make their music heard by more people. The remix album feels more like a continuation of the original project than a complement. Artists like Kelman Duran, Omaar, Siete Catorce, and DNZA take the tracks into unexpected territories. What criteria did you use to choose the collaborators? Were you specifically looking for them to reinterpret the material from perspectives very different from your own? The idea for the remix album came quite naturally because the original release was very short—it was only a cassette with a handful of tracks. Luis from Otono and I started talking about ways of expanding the project, and one of us suggested asking friends to reinterpret the music. It immediately felt like the right thing to do. I contacted the people I’m closest to musically and asked whether they’d be interested in remixing the EP. Rather than assigning specific tracks, I sent them the whole release and let each artist choose the piece they felt most connected to. I wanted everyone to work from genuine enthusiasm rather than obligation. Luis approached it from the other side. He reached out to artists through his own network, particularly musicians from Mexico, and he has a really good instinct for matching artists with material. In the end, it became a true collaboration—half through my connections, half through his. We also wanted to bring together people who have shaped what Latin American electronic music has become over the last decade. Fortunately, many of them are friends. Kelman Duran, for example, is someone I’m very close to. He came to Ecuador a couple of years ago and since then we’ve been constantly exchanging music and ideas. Siete Catorce is another artist I’ve admired for a long time. I think we’ve been in touch for more than ten years. I still remember hearing his music for the first time and thinking, “Wow, this is Latin American electronic music.” He was one of the artists who really opened that door for me. Luis also invited artists I deeply respect, like Omaar, as well as VIAAN, who is originally from Mexico and is now based in Berlin. Everyone involved already had a very distinctive musical identity, which was exactly what we wanted. None of the remixes tries to imitate the original tracks. Each one takes the material somewhere completely different while remaining connected to the spirit of the project. I think that’s why the remix album works so well—it doesn’t feel like an appendix to the original release. Every artist brings their own personality to the music, and the reinterpretations genuinely surprised me. You described these albums as a “message of Latin American unity.” At a time when much of experimental electronic music continues to look towards Europe or North America, your work draws on Indigenous and Afro-Ecuadorian traditions without turning them into folklore. What does this idea of ​​Latin American unity mean to you, both from a cultural and a musical point of view? That’s an interesting question because the idea actually came out of a political situation. Ecuador and Mexico went through a serious diplomatic crisis after our current president ordered the raid on the Mexican embassy in Quito. As a result, diplomatic relations were suspended. There is currently no Mexican embassy in Ecuador and no Ecuadorian embassy in Mexico. Luis, who runs Otono, is Mexican, and I’m Ecuadorian. We were watching all of this unfold while working together on these records. For us, the project became a way of saying that, despite what governments are doing, we’re still family. We’re making music together, exchanging ideas and building something collectively. That felt much more important than political divisions. At the same time, Latin America is going through a difficult moment. Across much of the continent, right-wing governments are cutting support for culture while aligning themselves politically with North America and Israel. Cultural funding is often the first thing to disappear, even when basic public services are already struggling. We wanted these records to carry a different message: that beyond politics we share histories, cultures and values that connect us across borders. Our societies are also becoming increasingly polarised. Everything seems reduced to left versus right, with very little room for dialogue. Music can remind us that there’s something else worth protecting. Every country has its own cultural identity, but those identities also speak to one another. That’s what I mean by Latin American unity. For centuries we’ve looked towards Europe or North America for artistic reference points. We absorbed ideas coming from elsewhere and adapted them to our own realities. Over the last fifteen or twenty years, though, something has begun to change. More and more artists are asking themselves: “Who are we? What stories belong to this place?” We live differently, we think differently and we experience the world differently. It’s time we started telling those stories ourselves instead of letting other people tell them for us. For me, that’s what finding a Latin American voice is really about. Finally, could you tell me a little about Ecuador’s experimental and electronic music scene? Outside Ecuador, very little is known about it. Ecuador actually has a much longer electronic music history than many people realise. The great pioneer is Mesías Maiguashca, who moved to Germany and worked with Karlheinz Stockhausen and many of the leading figures of European electronic music in the 1960s and ’70s. He’s someone every Ecuadorian working in experimental music looks up to. The problem is that it’s still very difficult to make a living from this kind of music in Ecuador. Most people simply don’t understand it. If you’re making ten-minute electroacoustic pieces full of strange sounds, they think you’re either wasting your time or completely crazy. There are only a handful of people making this kind of music. Artists like Quixosis, Joaquín Cornejo and a few others are doing really interesting work, but we’re talking about a very small community. Recently I’ve also seen some exciting initiatives around field recording. There are artists organising hikes into the mountains where participants record environmental sounds, then come back together to process the recordings and practise deep listening. I haven’t taken part myself, but I think it’s a wonderful idea because it encourages people to engage with the sonic environment in a completely different way. Most of this activity happens in Quito. I live in Ibarra, a small town about two or three hours away, and the local experimental scene is almost non-existent. There are maybe ten people interested in electroacoustic music here. Everyone else is listening to reggaeton and going out partying—which is completely fine—but it means experimental music remains very marginal. I actually came to this music through metal. I grew up listening to the darkest and heaviest metal I could find, especially black metal. Ambient black metal eventually led me towards electroacoustic music, and suddenly I realised there was this whole other way of thinking about sound. Once I discovered it, I couldn’t stop experimenting. What keeps me optimistic is that Ecuador is full of sounds that haven’t yet been explored. The musical traditions, the landscapes, the different cultures—there’s an almost infinite amount of material to work with. Experimental music here is still a very small field, but I think that’s exactly what makes it exciting. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 这张双专辑源自Esteban Farinango在厄瓜多尔Esmeraldas省Telembí社区的真实田野录音，将非裔厄瓜多尔传统节奏、马林巴琴、人声与田野采样融为一体，电子元素以低姿态介入，使原声表演与电子干预的边界逐渐模糊。Río Cayápas侧重社群、仪式与身体化的节奏，NXDLLI则将这些素材提炼为内省的电子声响景观，声音碎片保留着对原乡的记忆联结。附带的混音合辑呈现了记忆、梦境、解构低音、ambient drum & bass、footwork等多重再诠释路径。整体项目贯穿了对厄瓜多尔北部文化根源的追溯，电子与原声元素在共享空间中消解等级关系，是一次田野录音、实验电子与世界音乐交汇的深度实践。

items.body: Perhaps this new ROTCORE strata marks Batista’s next transmission. Here, rot does not simply signify decay; it becomes a productive process, a way for sounds to break down, recombine, and regrow. In that sense, IDM(R)ot I treats glitch not as damage to be corrected, but as evidence of life inside the machine—an opening through which IDM can mutate, regenerate, and find another generation of forms to cultivate and explore. Glitch becomes less an effect than a structural instinct ERR101: enabl.ed – IDM(R)ot I by enabl.ed   Clean Error label operator James Batista, a longtime IDM aficionado, continues to expand upon his enabl.ed moniker, a project that has spent years pursuing entangled electronics, glitch manifestations, and melodic fibers through another chapter, IDM(R)ot I. Detailed as ROTCORE, “developed to observe what happens to experimental music after its methods become part of a shared vocabulary,” Batista works at a high level of sonic fracture, clean errors, and digital misalignment, assembling a collection that “studies rhythm, synthesis, sequencing, sampling, digital processing, melodic behavior, structural irregularity, and intentional error.” Surrounded by a familiar cast of sonic crafters we tend to gravitate towards—ie. Cephlon, Romanowitch, Suumhow, Vaag, exm, rRine, Foel, Yaporigami, ENV(itre), Dragon, among others—enabl.ed finds its footing in disjointed rhythmic structures, where fifteen tracks lurch, stutter, flutter, and settle between lullaby tones and sharply articulated beats. Opener “initiate.rot.heirloom” immediately establishes this elegantly fractured language, allowing clipped rhythms and tiny digital disturbances to sit alongside softer melodic gestures. Batista’s sonic voice develops with remarkable consistency, even when the machinery catches on a few speed bumps, from the minuscule electro-entanglement of “rot.protocol\_113” to the roughened, shuffled beauty of “Reverb of a dead catalog.” Clean Error Records announces ERR101: enabl.ed — IDM(R)ot I, the next release in the label’s catalog and the beginning of a project examining the changing state of IDM through its history, production language and technological inheritance. Glitch becomes less an effect than a structural instinct throughout the record. Ambient threads seep through “time-stretched memories,” where stretched-out fragments seem suspended just beyond recognition, while “There are ghosts in the sequencer” digs into micro-textural repetition, letting clicks, granular debris, and sequencing artifacts accumulate into their own strange atmosphere. Earlier IDM signifiers surface across “time-stretched memories,” “Machine Empathy,” and “Failed Futurism,” yet each track pushes those familiar forms through enough processing, interruption, and rhythmic skew to keep them unstable. Melodies appear, fracture, loop, and mutate rather than simply resolve. Closer “Every genre contains its own extinction” hints at an even more pronounced shift in enabl.ed’s signature. Orchestral strings emerge amid organic glitch scurries in the background, creating a grandiose bookend unlike Batista’s earlier sound sculptures. What begins as digital fragmentation gradually opens into something more melancholic and cinematic, occupying an intersection between soundtrack music and IDM while remaining distinctly interstellar, tactile, and absorbing. Perhaps this new ROTCORE strata marks Batista’s next transmission. Here, rot does not simply signify decay; it becomes a productive process, a way for sounds to break down, recombine, and regrow. In that sense, IDM(R)ot I treats glitch not as damage to be corrected, but as evidence of life inside the machine—an opening through which IDM can mutate, regenerate, and find another generation of forms to cultivate and explore. ┌───────────────────────┐ │ R O T C O R E │ │ ERROR > IMITATION │ │ MUTATION > MEMORY │ └──────────┬────────────┘ │ ░▒▓████▓▒░ //│\ /// ERROR \\ //// BLOOMING \\ GENRE_CORRUPTION : 87.2% RHYTHM DECOMPOSITION : 74.8% MELODIC STABILITY : 41.3% ARCHIVE DEPENDENCY : CRITICAL NOSTALGIA SATURATION : HIGH ERROR VIABILITY : ██████████ IDM(R)ot I is available on Clean Error. [Bandcamp] The post enabl.ed :: IDM(R)ot I (Clean Error) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: enabl.ed 厂牌主理人 James Batista 在 Clean Error Records 厂牌发行专辑《IDM(R)ot I》，以 ROTCORE 为概念框架，审视实验音乐方法论被纳入通用语汇后所发生的变化。整张专辑围绕声音的碎裂、重组与再生展开，将故障视为机器内部生命力的证据，而非需要修正的损伤。十五首曲目在不连贯的节奏结构中摇摆，既有摇篮曲般的柔和音色，也有锐利的节拍切割。从极微观的电子缠绕到粗粝的洗牌美感，从拉伸到难以辨认的时间片段到序列器中幽灵般的微纹理重复，专辑不断让旋律出现、断裂、循环与变异，而非追求传统解决。Batista 的声音语言保持高度一致性，在熟悉的 IDM 信号标志之上注入足够的处理与节拍偏移，使形式始终处于不稳定状态，构成了对 IDM 自身历史与遗产的一次结构性反思。

items.body: Visible Light did not try to produce an exact sonic replica of El Yunque, but rather focused on the aspects that impacted the musicians the most, just as a landscape painter can highlight aspects of a landscape that a straightforward photo cannot communicate as well. “An act of ecological connection” Sierra de Luquillo: A Living Soundscape by Visible Light   Located on the slopes of the Sierra de Luquillo Mountains in northeastern Puerto Rico, El Yunque National Forest is the only tropical rainforest in the U.S. National Forest system. At almost 29,000 acres, El Yunque is one of our smallest national forests, yet it is also one of the most biologically diverse. For example, El Yunque hosts 250 different species of trees—about as many as are found throughout all our other national forests combined. Among other rare species, El Yunque provides one of the last remaining habitats for the critically endangered Puerto Rican Parrot. It also houses 13 of the 16 known species of the coqui frogs that Puerto Ricans have adopted as a symbol for themselves and their island. Yet a 2018 biological study found that global warming has reduced El Yunque’s arthropod (insect) biomass 10- to 60-fold, which in turn has led to corresponding declines in the lizards, frogs, birds and other creatures that feed upon these insects. Stunningly beautiful yet profoundly vulnerable, El Yunque serves as both a magnetic tourist destination and the home of the Indigenous Taino peoples’ chief god Yucahn (Yokahn). In February 2025, Minneapolis-based duo Visible Light visited El Yunque. Stunned by what they saw and heard, Amy McNally (cellist) and Matthew Hiram (sound artist) recorded many hours’ worth of nocturnal soundscapes in the forest and then shaped their own musical compositions in response. As Matthew Hiram wrote on his Substack, “the music was created in collaboration with El Yunque, as an act of ecological connection.” To me the resulting four-movement album feels like one extended meditation or deep listening event; it becomes difficult to tell where the natural sounds end and those of the human musicians begin. The album sounds almost like an acoustic version of the forest bathing contemplative nature walks that Japanese practitioners have introduced to the world. Calling the listener to pause and reflect :: And when Visible Light says they collaborated with El Yunque to make this music, they really mean it. In addition to the human instruments of cello, Moog synthesizers, rosewood alto flutes, sidereal gongs, brass singing bowls, and more, the voices of crickets, coqui frogs, and many other animals sing out on the album. And so do the voices of the plants themselves, captured by sensitive electrodes fitted to the plants’ leaves that pick up tiny electrical vibrations that are sent by MIDI to be processed and complemented, as Hiram has done on his solo albums like 2024’s Yucca Music.  Sierra de Luquillo begins with “La Oscuridad” (“The Darkness”), a more than 17-minute composition that is the longest on the album. Nocturnal keynotes of insects and coqui frogs take center stage, warmed by subtle cello and synth textures, calling the listener to pause and reflect on the peaceful beauty of wild places like El Yunque, to let it lighten and expand our souls. Later in the track the cello melodies sound almost in a call and response progression with the nocturnal animal voices, reminding me a bit of jazz musician and philosopher David Rothenberg’s famous duets with humpback whales on Whale Music. The next track, “Música de las Plants,” foregrounds plant voices. It begins again with the nocturnal sounds of coquis and insects, but now they sound closer, as if the listener’s ear is right up against the plants from which they are calling. Cello and synth melodies emerge and evolve subtly, almost like clouds passing in the sky above the forest. Then we start to hear the resonant hums converted from the bioelectrical signals sparking through the leaves of the plants. Developing slowly, the music moves at the more deliberate pace of the forest, not the heedless speed of the human world. Singing bowls add an ethereal, shimmering, almost spiritual layer to the processed plant vibrations. And even with all this emphasis on plant voices, those of animals remain foregrounded throughout, highlighting their importance and agency. Creating a tranquil, meditative, and spirit-expanding atmosphere :: “La Tormenta” (“The Storm”) focuses on a very common event for this tropical forest: rainfall, which it receives more than 6 meters (20 feet) of annually. On this track rumbling thunder and steady rain accompany the voices of coqui frogs, crickets, and other insects. I appreciate the percussive detail of individual raindrops colliding with leaves that emerges. Tasteful use of gongs extends the listener’s consciousness wider and deeper into the forest, helping focus our attention on darker aspects of the soundscape and how they resonate with our own inner spiritual depths—storms also roar within us at times, sometimes terrifyingly so, yet as with the outer rains in El Yunque, our own inner storms ultimately purify and renew us. I love how the coquis’ froggy voices sound almost joyous during the rainfall, reminding me of how the Prophet Muhammad described frogs as praising Allah with their croaks and cries. “Medianoche” (“Midnight”) closes the album. Here the insect and frog voices sound quieter, and the human synths and cello take center stage. The instruments do a lovely job expressing some of the uncanny, liminal quality of the midpoint of the night, which also holds the seeds of the dawn—a juxtaposition the listener can experience clearly on this track. There’s also a bit of a wistful feel to the cello, starting to bid farewell to this lovely wild and sacred place where even the local Indigenous Taino peoples did not traditionally dare to dwell for long. Rosewood flutes seem to express a kind of voice I wish we heard more of in the field recordings: the abundant bird life of the neotropics, complementing the cello in a lively back and forth that sounds like a vocal exchange between actual frogs and birds. The resulting warm sounds interspersed with heavy silences reminds me of how real animals listen to each other and to us just as much as we do them. Creating a tranquil, meditative, and spirit-expanding atmosphere, “Medianoche” makes for a lovely ending to this album. In the end I think Sierra de Luqillo does a great job of encouraging deep listening that can in turn cultivate a feeling of ecological connection, ideally leading the listener to practices of care and preservation. The compositions feel specific to this Puerto Rican place, with keynotes of frogs and insects and rain. Yet they also help the listener hear the importance of the natural places we inhabit wherever we are through newly attuned, more attentive ears. I also appreciated that Visible Light did not try to produce an exact sonic replica of El Yunque, but rather focused on the aspects that impacted the musicians the most, just as a landscape painter can highlight aspects of a landscape that a straightforward photo cannot communicate as well. Sierra de Luquillo: A Living Soundscape is available on Bandcamp. Sierra de Luquillo: A Living Soundscape by Visible Light The post Visible Light :: Sierra de Luquillo: A Living Soundscape (Permaculture Media) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: 双人组合Visible Light于2025年前往波多黎各的El Yunque雨林，在夜间录制大量环境声景素材，并以此为基础进行再创作。大提琴、Moog合成器、紫檀中音长笛、星体锣、黄铜颂钵等人声乐器与蟋蟀、青蛙等动物声响交织融合。专辑最突出的创新在于通过电极捕捉植物叶片释放的微弱电振动，经MIDI转化为可听声波，将植物本身的声音纳入音乐结构，实现真正意义上的生态协作。四乐章构成一场深度聆听仪式，模糊了自然声与人工乐器演奏的边界。Permaculture Media为独立小厂牌，整体呈现介于环境音乐、田野录音与当代古典之间的混合美学，强调对脆弱生态系统的感知与回应。

items.body: MEGAFAUNA creates a dark atmosphere using nature sounds and electro-acoustic manipulation to take the mind somewhere it didn’t expect to go. Listening to this at early morning hours, at normal volume, lying down, not fully awake, is a specific and disorienting experience. It’s quite amazing for what it is: a live improvisation built from birds that manages to sound like a horror score composed by the landscape itself. A strength in honest field recording work and a meticulous approach to effects Birdsong by MEGAFAUNA   MEGAFAUNA is a project based out of Hazelton, British Columbia, a small town in Northern BC’s Skeena Country, deep in a landscape of mountains, rivers, and boreal wilderness. Operating under the self-described tag “despairtronica,” the project has built a catalog of IDM-influenced and breakcore-adjacent electronic music characterized by hard drums, fast tempos, and dense sonic construction. A September release is on the horizon that will return to that territory. Birdsong is something else entirely, and that contrast is part of what makes it worth paying attention to. The field recording and bioacoustics tradition has a long and serious history. Bernie Krause—one of the foremost soundscape ecologists alive, has spent over fifty years recording natural soundscapes and coined the term “soundscape ecology,” documenting how the sonic layers of an environment (biophony, geophony, anthrophony) create a complete acoustic picture of a habitat’s health. The Cornell Lab of Ornithology‘s Macaulay Library holds over 175,000 audio recordings of wildlife going back to 1929, including the world’s oldest known wildlife sound recordings. Ornithological vocalization analysis—the study of bird calls for species identification, territorial behavior, and mating patterns, is a genuine scientific discipline. What MEGAFAUNA does here isn’t science. But it borrows from the same raw material and pushes it somewhere considerably darker. Birdsong was commissioned by circumstance, an invitation to perform at the Midsummer Music Festival in Smithers, British Columbia, with a specific request for something more ethereal than the prior year’s set. The response was a 42:42 improvised piece built entirely from bird call samples, performed live on July 4th, 2026, with rain and thunder added afterward to reflect what was literally happening before, during, and after the performance in real life. The track listing credits specific birds by role—percussion (Shoebill, Crested Caracara, Lyrebird), vox (Quail, Three Wattled Bellbird, Bearded Bellbird, Capuchin, Horned Screamer, Screaming Piha), ambience (Common Loon, Helmeted Hornbill, Pheasant Coucal, Tawny Frogmouth), melody (Raven, Australian Bustard, American Bittern, Common Starling, Magpie), and keyboard (Crow). Whether this is satire, creative taxonomy, or a genuine documentation of sources used, it’s a uniquely compelling framing device that makes the listener hear the piece differently, starting to identify what each bird might be contributing to the overall texture. What MEGAFAUNA shows with “Birdsong” is a strength in honest field recording work and a meticulous approach to effects, how carefully FX are applied to these recordings and how that compositional process produces something genuinely interesting. None of it is repetitive. These are natural sounds being manipulated very carefully with dark ambience throughout. None of the atmosphere on this release is pleasant, it presents itself as a dark record, which is also what makes it strangely unique. When you think of birds, darkness isn’t the first association, unless you’re thinking of vultures or birds of prey. But MEGAFAUNA pulls darkness out of unexpected sources. The Horned Screamer and Screaming Piha are doing exactly what their names suggest, and pitched down and ring modulated, they become something else entirely. The first two minutes present something resembling a rainforest, birds layering and overlapping in what sounds like natural habitat. Then around the 3:30 mark, things shift. The atmosphere darkens and stays dark, little bursts of FX being applied to various bird calls, distortions and pitching manipulations building until the 23-minute mark where something changes audibly. A pitch-bending melody arrives like an echoing alarm, a new segment of birds being introduced, the composition pivoting into its second movement. At the 27:40 mark, another sound surfaces that reads initially as an alarm but is clearly a bird call being manipulated—low pitched, ring modulated, buried under heavy reverb, looping in a way that creates something deeply unsettling and hard to source. It’s the kind of sound that makes you question what you’re hearing. The FX work is what really stands out, the ability to keep ears engaged with bird calls and sounds for 42 minutes without the piece becoming monotonous is a genuine compositional achievement. MEGAFAUNA creates a dark atmosphere using nature sounds and electro-acoustic manipulation to take the mind somewhere it didn’t expect to go. Listening to this at early morning hours, at normal volume, lying down, not fully awake, is a specific and disorienting experience. It’s quite amazing for what it is: a live improvisation built from birds that manages to sound like a horror score composed by the landscape itself. Birdsong is available on Bandcamp. Birdsong by MEGAFAUNAThe post MEGAFAUNA :: Birdsong (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: MEGAFAUNA 来自加拿大不列颠哥伦比亚省北部的哈兹尔顿，以"绝望电子乐"自居，此前作品以硬鼓、快节奏的智能舞曲和碎核风格为主。《Birdsong》是一次彻底的转向：全长四十二分钟，全部由鸟鸣采样构建，2026年7月在斯米瑟斯仲夏音乐节现场即兴演奏，随后叠加上演出前后实际发生的雨声与雷声。评论将作品比作"由景观本身谱写的恐怖配乐"，强调其在清晨半梦半醒时聆听产生的失衡感与黑暗氛围。曲目按鸟种分配功能——打击乐、人声、和声、旋律、键盘——这种独特的编目方式为作品增添了概念层面的趣味。整体上，这是一张以田野录音为原材料、经过细致效果处理的实验作品，介于声音艺术、环境音乐与暗黑电子之间，与听者口味高度契合。

items.body: AkA is a project founded by Frenchman Henri Sizaret. Now based in Portugal, AkA has a career spanning more than 30 years. This new release comprises nine tracks conceived as a form of litany. AkA’s musical world is fascinating yet difficult to pin down. Primarily an Electronic project, this album sits somewhere between Ambient and Experimental music, with various other influences surfacing from time to time. While the sound is at times minimalist, the compositions remain intelligent, with meticulous attention paid to every sound, effect, and field recording. Slow rhythms occasionally emerge, making the music more accessible. Vocals also feature prominently, delivered in various languages and a spoken format, or even whispered. This fits perfectly with the album’s atmosphere: mysterious and cold. A few tracks also incorporate female choral vocals, carefully sampled and blended into the background. AkA offers a unique experience, delivering visionary Electronic music, and “Echo Ex Voto” is a brilliant example of this. (Rating:8½). Listen to “Under Your Protection”: https://akamuzik.bandcamp.com/track/under-your-protection

items.body: A favorite from last year was Spirits of the Dead Are Watching, the debut of Believe, the Sydney-based quartet of Peter Farrar (saxophone), Novak Manojlovic (piano), Clayton Thomas (bass), and Laurence Pike (drums). Believe arrived as a mature working group, having largely negotiated their aesthetic off-tape. There's much care in their improvisations, which convey a particular reverence for the heightened space that opens when people play music together. All of the musicians doubled on small percussion instruments, and even when it got intense, the music had a ceremonial air, the band unafraid of rhythm and repetition, staying with fertile moments and drawing them out like silken filaments. That introduction was often a work of tension or calling-to-attention, and their follow-up, Nature's God —culled from the same 2023 recording sessions—feels more contemplative. It initially did not grab me in the same way, but I'm in its grip now. That first encounter was a victim of my own lack of care. Listening to Nature's God, one of the first things I noticed—or rather, one of the things that allowed much to escape notice during my initial distracted listen—is the sparse appearance of Farrar's saxophone. On the opening title track, he doesn't pick it up at all. The music develops from hushed notes with a sly and simmering urgency, Pike and Manojlovic goading each other along, the whole thing less a dramatic revelation than the dawning realization that the looming intensity of its namesake is always already present. Setting the saxophone down in favor of percussion reduces the instrumental contrast and further heightens the feeling of a collective sound, particularly in combination with Thomas's often percussive bass playing, striking the strings with mallets or its body with his hands. "Braided River" is a prayer, as beautiful and coherent a thing as free improvisation can produce, the saxophone arising and Thomas and Farrar so close in tone and intent that they're indeed braided into a new, quavering timbre. With the exception of the almost jazzy centerpiece "First Name Of A Flower" (which works itself into a fairly swinging groove by its midpoint), the pieces on Nature's God further underscore the ritualistic leanings that made Believe's debut so interesting. Small changes accrue but the music remains whole, like an undulating shape. Sometimes this takes the form of repetitive motifs or textures, as in Farrar's long tones and Manojlovic's delicate figures in the aforementioned "Braided River." At other times it is expressed in more explicit rhythm, such as the steadfast beat driving "Earth Does Not Need Us," the axis of a polyrhythmic swirl. Closing piece "Owls" is daybreak, that transition when the owls have settled and are handing the world back to the day dwellers. Again, no saxophone. The shimmering piano notes hang like dewdrops in a web, and every note, whatever the source, is allowed its full measure. At one point a flare of feedback breaks through, and for some reason I think of sunlight rising through dripping trees, of the moment a ray first strikes your eye and, although it is all so beautiful, you have to look away. items._cn_summary: 这张由悉尼四人组合 Believe 录制的《Nature's God》延续了其首张专辑的精神脉络，展现出更为内省冥想的特质。乐评指出专辑最显著的特点是萨克斯的稀疏使用，Peter Farrar 在多首曲目中放下主乐器改用小型打击乐器，使得整体音色更趋统一与仪式化。Thomas 的贝斯演奏带有强烈的打击性，常以槌击弦或手掌拍击琴身，强化了集体音响的氛围。曲目如《Braided River》如祷词般绵长，Farrar 与 Thomas 在音色与意图上紧密交织，形成颤动的全新质感；《Owls》以无萨克斯的钢琴独奏收尾，音符如晨露般悬挂于蛛网之上。整张专辑呈现出对重复与节奏的坦然拥抱，每一处细微变化缓慢累积，音乐整体如同一个起伏的完整形态，倾向于仪式感与精神性。

items.body: Spanish, Berlin-based Irene Aranda is primarily a classically trained pianist and self-taught in free jazz and free improvisation hyper-pianist who employs the piano as a sonic environment, using preparations and extended techniques to uncover enigmatic textures and resonances. Irene Aranda - MAY (Relative Pitch, 2026) MAY features Aranda in a trio with Spanish sax player Don Malfon (aka Alfonso Muñoz) and Japanese-born vocal (and visual) artist Ami Yamasaki in a studio recording from Berlin in January 2026. The eight free improvised pieces are titled as wishes that begin with “May the games begin”, go through “May you have many more meaning in Urdu”, and end with “May you all hate free jazz” (apparently, with the most free jazz playing by Aranda here). This unconventional trio take their respective singular sonic palettes of Malfon, Aranda, and Yamasaki to the extreme, obviously, with an array of highly personal extended techniques - breathing (with mutes and objects, in the case of Malfon), echolocation vocals (Yamasaki), and playing (or pounding) inside the piano (Aranda). Each piece visits a distinct, intense, and deeply visceral, immersive territory, shaped by radical, urgent, and Dadaist approaches to breath, space, vibration, or sound at all, often on the verge of chaos. The trio keeps searching for friction and compatibility of its strong-minded musical personalities. Occasionally, the trio’s dark humour and Yamasaki’s sensual, lyrical, and often pixie-like (wordless) voice introduce a more accessible vein into the uncompromising sonic collisions. There is no end to the inventive, inimitable dynamics of this trio or to its unpredictable, captivating lexicon. Prepare for the most physical, wildest possible ride yet a highly rewarding one where even the most discerning listeners may find themselves caught off guard. MAY by Irene Aranda The Dark Deniers - Tales of Freedom (Self-Released, 2026) Aranda leaves the piano aside and is the mastermind, conductor, vocalist and bandleader of The Dark Deniers ensemble, a Berlin-based experimental octet featuring trumpeters Germán García and Brad Henkel, alto sax player Grgur Savić, baritone sax player Pablo Muñoz, trombonist Gerhard Gschlößl, guitarist Christian Kühn, and drummer Martial Frenzel. The Dark Deniers mix dramatic poetic texts (of John Masefield, Maya Angelou, John Donne, Lord Byron, Antonio Machado, Alfonsina Storni, Anne Bradstreet, Paul Éluard, Gilbert Chesterton, and Dylan Thomas), focusing on mortality, resistance, existential collapse, time, and transformation, with Butch Morris’ conduction principle, free jazz, avant-rock, metal, and free improvisation. The Dark Deniers’ debut album, Tales of Freedom , was recorded live at Studio Zentri Fuge in Berlin in May 2026. Aranda is a capable, evocative and passionate vocalist and a commanding leader who leads this organism-like, powerful ensemble through ten pieces, beginning with the ritualist, pagan-like prayer (or provocation): “We are The Dark Deniers. Let us summon Death from a summer woman”, and soon lets this poetic phrase bloom into a funky storm. This ensemble sounds as if it searches for a primordial, pre-cosmic state of raw sound, as expressed in the aptly titled “Vocifera”, with Aranda’s effective growling vocals. Throughout Tales of Freedom , Aranda uses the poetic texts, the language (the English, Spanish, and French ones), and the ensemble’s complex sonic palettes as material she can shape, mould, and invent anew as impossible yet intricate, organic structures, with a touching, thought-provoking, and often subversive pathos. The Dark Deniers, like the trio with Malfon and Yamasaki, also embrace chaos, but in a different approach. Aranda shapes the sonic architectures and literary texts from chaos and sheer visceral freedom, and vice versa, always flirting joyfully with fiery, explosive dynamics, danger and risk-taking, or as Aranda puts it: “play with death the way that children play with fire”. Any round with Aranda’s music is bound to take listeners on the most unpredictable yet deeply immersive wild ride, inspire and equip us all with enough invigorating food for resisting thoughts, until, one day, Aranda and The Dark Deniers will rule the world. The Dark Deniers - Tales of Freedom by Irene Aranda Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 本文评介西班牙钢琴家Irene Aranda的两张专辑。其一为与萨克斯手Don Malfon及声音艺术家Ami Yamasaki组成的三重奏《MAY》，八首曲目以祈愿句式命名，从准备钢琴、扩展技巧到人声回声定位，三位演奏家将各自独特声响推向极端，在呼吸、空间与振动中构建激烈而沉浸的声景。Yamasaki的空灵人声偶尔透出可接近性，平衡了整体的激进碰撞。其二为Aranda以乐队领袖身份领导的八人实验乐团The Dark Deniers首作《Tales of Freedom》，融合Butch Morris指挥法、自由爵士、前卫摇滚、金属与即兴，选用多位诗人的诗作文本，主题涉及死亡、抵抗与时间蜕变，录音于柏林现场。整体呈现高度实验性、跨文化与跨语境的创作路径。

items.body:
The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑聚焦荷兰低音提琴手Arjen Gorter的音乐生涯，尤其是他与Willem Breuker Kollektief长期合作的经历，同时也涵盖他独立发展的脉络。乐评以详实的口述历史展开：从阿姆斯特丹街头的手风琴、尤克里里，到偶然接触的贝斯，Gorter的乐器之路充满偶然与直觉。他自1966年起与Breuker合作，参与了首张录音《Litany for the 14th of June 1966》，并在随后数十年间成为该团体低音根基的支柱。文中还提及他与德国自由爵士萨克斯手Gunter Hampel的合作，展示了他在Kollektief框架之外的即兴探索。整篇乐评更偏向档案式的口述史与人物梳理，而非纯粹的音乐分析，但为欧洲前卫爵士场景中的低音提琴传承提供了珍贵的文献视角。

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.

items._cn_summary: 这是一篇关于集体即兴音乐的乐评，涵盖两场二重奏和两场四重奏录音，跨越十二年时间线。作者强调近距离聆听与同步写作的结合所产生的语言碰撞，暗示这些作品中集体创作所引发的转化性复杂性与重叠视野。评论特别详细介绍了Emilio Gordoa与已故Sven-Åke Johansson的二重奏专辑《Die Dritte Ebene》，两位音乐家探讨了音乐如何在平行线般的运动中产生某种第三层幽灵般的神秘涌现。音乐让人联想到萨蒂的家具音乐，构成一种提升意识的激进背景音乐，通过重复材料的特殊共鸣创造恍惚而近乎出神的状态，在演奏者与听众的协作中产生难以言喻的灵性焦点。评论整体充满哲思，探讨即兴音乐如何超越语言边界，成为来自未知文化、献给未知神明的赞美诗。

items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.

items._cn_summary: Ran Blake以独特的选曲和手法区别于过去六十余年的任何创新钢琴家。他能将看似毫不相关的作品并置，从Max Roach到Michel Legrand，从民谣到Whitney Houston的流行金曲，像MRI一样揭示音乐内部隐藏的连接组织。Dominique Eade的演唱是专辑核心，她不依赖Billie Holiday式的根脉，也不刻意内敛，而是以逐音节的雕琢和饱满的喜悦感呈现歌曲——无论明亮的流行大作还是Charles Mingus的阴郁肖像曲，都渗透着她对歌唱本身的热爱。这种另辟蹊径的人声处理超越了Blake与Jeanne Lee经典合作的光环框架，使专辑在学院爵士框架内展现出罕见的跨界选材与个人化诠释。

items.body: Pakistani-American composer Qasim Naqvi is about to drop a debut solo album on Erased Tapes. Naqvi isn’t a stranger to the label (he plays drums in Dawn of Midi), and his modular synths are living, breathing things. He’s an expert at bringing the synth out of its shell, not that it needs any encouragement. Like a raging teenager, the synth can’t be completely tamed, giving the music a spark of raw electricity, but Naqvi has the skill to reel it in from time to time, offering incentives and telling it to go to its room when it’s acting a little naughty. Naqvi manages to keep it on its leash even as said leash continues to strain and fray, the synth tugging on the music like a dog that’s just seen a squirrel scampering up a tree. Teenages is set in a dark park, though. Although it won’t be arrested for committing antisocial behaviour offences and no stabbings have ever been reported, it goes through a six-year teenage cycle over a run of six tracks. It’s a long and painful episode of defining change, growing pains, relationship-blurs, bad decisions that turn out to be lessons and opportunities for learning, and prolonged periods of phone use, eventually developing into a unique, beatless creature. Sure, there aren’t any drums. But you can have a rhythm without a beat. And this is a rhythmic album, entering through a line of strobing synths, with their patterns, pulses, and intermittent blips replacing the thump of a nightclub beat. Sometimes rolling off the tongue with a series of light trip-e-lets, and at other times tripping up on seemingly nothing but air and space, the young synths seem to be in their element here, roaming together as a group of friends, enjoying themselves and their nightly wanderings, cruising the streets with in-shape and steel-strong physiques to rival the mannequins in a Gap store. They’ll only become stronger as exam season ends and school closes for a mammoth eight weeks, to the tune of Alice Cooper’s eternal declaration and an inflated increase of plays on Spotify. Like a finely-tuned muscle, the synth is resolute but flexible, and its features pale underneath a ghost-white moon. On the title track – which is a winding, sprawling eighteen minutes – notes stutter, lighting up one after another like a UFO hidden deep within thick woodland. Its light-gang comes to life and burns in sequence, but it shifts around in other, lesser-known areas, taking the music away from a popular make-out spot and into darker territory. Naqvi’s music is transcendent and translucent, taking flight with spinning-top wobbles and gravity-defying lift-offs. If you’re looking for a record of transformative synth, Teenages is for you. Just don’t tell mom. www.erasedtapes.com
